title: Linear Accelerator
short_intro: A linear accelerator (Linac) is a particle accelerator that propels charged particles to high speeds along a straight linear path by applying a series of oscillating electric potentials. It avoids the energy losses due to synchrotron radiation that plague circular accelerators.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic working principle of particle acceleration, drift tube arrangement (Alvarez type), and simple resonance conditions.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed mathematical derivation of drift tube lengths, phase stability, transit-time factor, and relativistic energy considerations.

prerequisites: Motion of charged particles in uniform and alternating electric fields
Radio frequency (RF) oscillators and electromagnetic wave resonance

concept_notes.heading: Working Principle of Drift Tube Linac (Alvarez Structure)
bullets: Consists of a sequence of hollow cylindrical metal tubes (drift tubes) placed inside a resonant cavity along a common axis.
Alternating radio-frequency (RF) voltage is applied between successive drift tubes, creating an accelerating electric field in the gaps.
Inside the drift tubes, the electric field is zero (shielding effect), so particles coast at a constant velocity without deceleration during the retarding half-cycle.

concept_notes.heading: Phase Stability and Bunching
bullets: Particles must arrive at the accelerating gaps when the RF electric field has the correct magnitude and direction.
Synchronous particles arrive at an equilibrium phase angle where they gain the exact design energy per gap.
Particles arriving slightly early or late experience restoring electric forces that bunch them around the synchronous phase, ensuring beam stability.

concept_notes.heading: Velocity and Length Progression of Drift Tubes
bullets: As the charged particle gains kinetic energy across each gap, its velocity increases progressively.
To maintain synchronism with the constant RF frequency, each successive drift tube must be made longer than the preceding one.
The length of the n-th drift tube is proportional to the particle velocity at that stage.

concept_notes.heading: Advantages and Limitations
bullets: Eliminates synchrotron radiation losses, allowing very high energy electrons to be accelerated cleanly.
Can achieve extremely high beam currents and is widely used for medical therapy and as injectors for synchrotrons.
Physical length can become excessively large for very high energies, requiring immense real estate.

derivations.title: Derivation of Drift Tube Length
derivations.conditions: Non-relativistic charged particle of mass m and charge q accelerated by an RF oscillator of frequency f.
steps: Let v_n be the velocity of the particle after passing through n gaps. The time taken to traverse the n-th drift tube of length L_n is t_n = L_n / v_n.
For synchronism, this transit time must be equal to half the period of the RF oscillation: t_n = T / 2 = 1 / (2f).
Equating the two expressions for time: L_n / v_n = 1 / (2f), which gives the length of the n-th drift tube as L_n = v_n / (2f).

derivations.title: Total Kinetic Energy after N Gaps
derivations.conditions: Particle starting from rest with charge q and passing through N identical gaps with peak potential V_0.
steps: The energy gained in a single gap is given by \Delta E = q V_0 \cos\phi_s, where \phi_s is the synchronous phase angle.
Assuming the phase angle is adjusted such that \cos\phi_s \approx 1 for maximum acceleration, the energy gained per gap is q V_0.
For N acceleration gaps, the total kinetic energy accumulated by the particle is the product of the number of gaps and the energy gain per gap.

solved_numericals.question: In a linear accelerator, protons are accelerated through a series of gaps. If the peak voltage across each gap is 100 kV and there are 50 gaps, calculate the total kinetic energy gained by a proton in MeV.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Number of gaps N = 50, Peak voltage V_0 = 100 kV = 10^5 V, Charge of proton q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} C.
Apply total energy formula: E = N q V_0.
Substitute values: E = 50 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19} C) \times (10^5 V) = 8 \times 10^{-13} J.
Convert joules to MeV: E = (8 \times 10^{-13}) / (1.6 \times 10^{-13}) = 5 MeV.

solved_numericals.question: Find the length of the 4th drift tube in a linear accelerator operating at an RF frequency of 200 MHz, given that a proton has attained a velocity of 3 \times 10^7 m/s at that stage.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: Frequency f = 200 MHz = 2 \times 10^8 Hz, Velocity v_4 = 3 \times 10^7 m/s.
Use the drift tube length formula for the n-th tube: L_n = v_n / (2f).
Substitute the given values: L_4 = (3 \times 10^7) / (2 \times 2^8 \times 10^6 ... wait, 2 \times 200 \times 10^6) = (3 \times 10^7) / (4 \times 10^8).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the mass of an electron required to reach a relativistic velocity where its total energy is 10 times its rest mass energy inside a linear accelerator, given rest mass m_0 = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} kg.
solution_steps: Relativistic total energy is given by E = \gamma m_0 c^2.
Given condition: E = 10 E_0 = 10 m_0 c^2, which implies the Lorentz factor \gamma = 10.
Relativistic mass m is related to rest mass by m = \gamma m_0.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes uniform electric field across the accelerating gaps, neglecting fringe field effects at high frequencies.
Non-relativistic formulas fail at very high energies where particle velocities approach the speed of light, requiring velocity-dependent relativistic corrections for drift tube sizing.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Particles are accelerated while passing through the interior of the drift tubes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Particles are shielded inside the drift tubes and experience zero electric field; acceleration occurs only across the gaps between tubes.
common_misconceptions.why: Electrostatic shielding inside hollow conductors ensures no net electric force acts on the particle inside the drift tube.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All drift tubes in a linear accelerator have the exact same length.
common_misconceptions.correct: Drift tubes must progressively increase in length as the particle speeds up to maintain synchronism with the fixed RF frequency.
common_misconceptions.why: Since velocity increases after each gap, a longer tube is required to maintain the correct half-period traversal time.

quick_revision: Linacs accelerate charged particles along a straight line using RF electric fields across alternating drift tube gaps, avoiding synchrotron radiation losses.
Total Kinetic Energy: E = N q V_0
